title: Double treble
subtitle: A tall, open stitch, called treble crochet in the United States
excerpt: The double treble is taller than the treble, made with two yarn-overs at the start and worked off in three steps. Dillmont called it the long stitch. It builds airy, fast-growing fabric and the deep posts of lace edgings.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the passage on double trebles, which Dillmont also names the long stitch (Fig. 418). Public domain via Project Gutenberg. UK and US stitch-name equivalences cross-checked against the Craft Yarn Council standard terms.

glossaryTerms.definition: A tall crochet stitch made with two yarn-overs before the hook goes in, then worked off two loops at a time in three steps. Taller than a treble. The UK name; called treble crochet in the United States.
The United States name for the stitch British patterns call a double treble. The steps are identical; only the name differs.
Wrapping the working yarn over the hook from back to front before working a stitch. A double treble takes two wraps before the hook goes in.

content.text: The
double treble
is a tall, open stitch, one step up from the treble. You make two wraps of
yarn round hook

before the hook goes in, then work the loops off two at a time over three steps. The result is a deep post that grows fabric fast and sits airy. Dillmont called it the long stitch; in the United States it is called
treble crochet

attrs.alt: Engraving of double trebles in a row, showing the long posts each crossed by two horizontal bars.
attrs.title: Fig. 418, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (Thérèse de Dillmont, 1886). Public domain.

content.text: How to form the stitch
Begin with one working loop on the hook.
Wrap the yarn over the hook twice.
Insert the hook into the next stitch or chain.
Wrap the yarn over and draw a loop back through. Four loops sit on the hook.
Wrap the yarn over and pull through the first two loops. Three loops remain.
Wrap the yarn over and pull through the next two loops. Two loops remain.
Wrap the yarn over and pull through the last two loops. One loop is left, and the double treble is done.
At the start of a row, four chains stand in for the first double treble.
Where you will use it

Double trebles give lace its height. They make the deep openwork of shawls, the tall mesh of filet panels, and the long posts that fan out in shell edgings. Worked alone they grow a light, drapey fabric quickly; worked in groups they make the airy clusters of openwork patterns. Where a treble is too short to give the open look a pattern wants, the double treble steps in.
Variations and related stitches

Add a third wrap at the start and you get a triple treble, taller again. The treble is the shorter neighbour. Worked in clusters joined at the top, double trebles make tall bobbles and open fans. Because the post is long, keeping each pull-through even matters more than with shorter stitches, or the fabric leans.
Difficulty: intermediate. The steps are the same idea as a treble, just two more pulls to keep track of.
